arXiv:1410.5862v2 [math.DG] 30 Sep 2015

Surveying points in the complex projective plane

Lane Hughston and Simon Salamon

We classify SIC-POVMs of rank one in ℂ​ℙ2,\mathbb{CP}^{2}, or equivalently sets of nine equally-spaced points in ℂ​ℙ2,\mathbb{CP}^{2}, without the assumption of group covariance. If two points are fixed, the remaining seven must lie on a pinched torus that a standard moment mapping projects to a circle in ℝ3.\mathbb{R}^{3}. We use this approach to prove that any SIC set in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} is isometric to a known solution, given by nine points lying in triples on the equators of the three 2-spheres each defined by the vanishing of one homogeneous coordinate. We set up a system of equations to describe hexagons in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} with the property that any two vertices are related by a cross ratio (transition probability) of 1/4.1/4. We then symmetrize the equations, factor out by the known solutions, and compute a Gröbner basis to show that no SIC sets remain. We do find new configurations of nine points in which 27 of the 36 pairs of vertices of the configuration are equally spaced.

Introduction

A symmetric, informationally complete, positive-operator valued measure or SIC-POVM on the Hermitian vector space ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} is a set {Pj}\{P_{j}\} of n2n^{2} rank-one projection operators such that

1n​∑i=1n2Pi=I,\frac{1}{n}\!\sum_{i=1}^{n^{2}}P_{i}=I,

and

tr(Pj​Pk)=1n+1​(n​δj​k+1)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(P_{j}P_{k})=\frac{1}{n+1}(n\delta_{jk}+1)

for all j,k.j,k. Such objects attracted wide attention following conjectures about their existence made by Zauner [43] in 1999 and Renes et al. [32] in 2004, and since then have been investigated by a large number of authors, along with higher rank versions and the allied concept of mutually unbiased basis. See, for example, [2, 3, 4, 11, 13, 17, 18, 21, 24, 33, 42, 44], and references cited therein.

SIC-POVMs arise in the theory of quantum measurement (see Davies [12] and Holevo [22] for the significance of general POVMs), and are of great interest in connection with their potential applications to quantum tomography. The idea is the following. Suppose that one has a large number of independent identical copies of a quantum system (say, a large molecule), the state (or ‘structure’) of which is unknown and needs to be determined. A SIC-POVM can be thought of as a kind of symmetrically oriented machine that can be used to make a single tomographic measurement on each independent copy of the molecule, with the property that once the results of the various measurements have been gathered for a sufficiently large number of molecules, the state of the molecule can be efficiently determined to a high degree of accuracy. The ‘symmetric orientation’ is not with respect to ordinary three-dimensional physical space (as in the classical tomography of medical imaging), but rather with respect to the space of pure quantum states.

Since each element PiP_{i} of a SIC-POVM is a matrix of rank one and trace unity, it determines a point in complex projective space ℂ​ℙn−1.\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}. It is well known that a SIC-POVM can then be defined as a configuration of n2n^{2} points in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} that are mutually equidistant under the standard Kähler metric [29, 39]. This is the definition that we shall adopt in §3, and the distance is determined by Lemma 3.6. Such a set of points is often called a ‘SIC’, but we favour the expression ‘SIC set’.

The existence of such configurations (for example, nine equidistant points in ℂ​ℙ2,\mathbb{CP}^{2}, or sixteen equidistant points in ℂ​ℙ3\mathbb{CP}^{3}) is counterintuitive to our everyday way of thinking in which a regular simplex in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has n+1n+1 vertices (but see [19]). It has been conjectured that ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} possesses such a configuration for every nn [32, 43]. There is evidence for this for nn up to at least 67,67, and various explicit solutions have been found in lower dimensions. Most of the known SIC sets in higher dimensions are constructed as orbits of a Heisenberg group W×HW\times H acting on ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} (see Section 3), and representative vectors occur as eigenvectors of an isometry that is an outer automorphism of W×H.W\times H. In the case n=5n=5, the automorphisms of W×HW\times H play a key role in the construction of the celebrated Horrocks-Mumford bundle over ℂ​ℙ4\mathbb{CP}^{4} in [23], which is an excellent reference for this group theory. In the case n=3n=3 (and more generally, when nn is prime) any finite group of isometries whose orbit is a SIC set must be conjugate to W×HW\times H [44], but in this paper we work without the assumption of group covariance (see Grassl [18]).

The space ℂ​ℙ1,\mathbb{CP}^{1}, endowed with the Fubini-Study metric, is isometric to the standard two-sphere, and embedding this in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} is a simple example of the representation of ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} as an adjoint orbit in the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔲​(n)\mathfrak{su}(n) of its isometry group. The existence of a SIC set can then be interpreted as a statement about the placement of such orbits. The problem can also be formulated so as to apply to more general (co-)adjoint orbits in a Lie algebra.

The vertices of any inscribed regular tetrahedron in S2S^{2} provide a SIC set for ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} (n=2n=2). The situation for the projective plane ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} is already surprisingly intricate, and the case n=3n=3 is characterized by the existence of continuous families of non-congruent SIC sets. It is easy to begin their study. Using homogeneous coordinates, any three equally-spaced points on the equator {[0,z2,z3]:|z2|=|z3|}\{[0,z_{2},z_{3}]:|z_{2}|=|z_{3}|\} of the two-sphere z1=0z_{1}=0 lie in a SIC set formed by adding three equally-spaced points from each of the equators of the two-spheres z2=0z_{2}=0 and z3=0.z_{3}=0. If the diameter of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} is chosen to be π,\pi, all nine points are a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 apart. Moreover, if the three triples match up so as to lie on a total of twelve projective lines, the nine points are the flexes of a plane cubic curve [24].

In this paper, we show that any SIC set in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} is congruent to one of those just described (see Theorem 5.5). This result will not surprise the experts; it has perhaps been verified numerically, and is apparently a consequence of computer-aided results in [36]. Our proof relies on a computation for its final step but is predominantly analytical. We use the two-point homogeneity of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} to fix two points of a SIC set; applying the moment mapping relative to a maximal torus shows that the remaining seven points lie in a pinched torus above a circle 𝒞\mathscr{C} in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} (illustrated in Figure 1). We exhibit the known solutions in a different form (Proposition 6.2) and characterize them by a symmetry condition (Lemma 8.2). Adding three more points a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 from the first two and from each other leads to a polynomial equation that is symmetric in three variables x,y,zx,y,z that represent the tangents of angles measured around 𝒞\mathscr{C} (Theorem 7.3). The resulting geometry is illustrated in Section 8.

Adding a sixth point allows us to write down four equations in four variables t,x,y,z.t,x,y,z. When these are totally symmetrized, we obtain a system that represents a necessary condition for the six points to form part of a SIC set. For the known solutions, at least one of the four points on the pinched torus must project to 𝒞\mathscr{C} with an angle equal to ±π/6.\pm\pi/6. This fact enables us to focus attention on the so-called quotient ideal that parametrizes ‘extra’ solutions, and to describe it by means of an appropriate Gröbner basis. Once one root tt is fixed, the extra solutions form a finite set and the final step is to determine its size. There are too few extra solutions for these to arise from an undiscovered SIC set.

This paper had its origins in a number of survey talks aimed at bringing elements of the SIC-POVM problem in various low dimensions to the attention of a wider audience, and the title and figures reflect this. We focus on the case n=3n=3 from Section 4 onwards, and Sections 6–10 contain the more specialized material required to achieve our goal. The Fubini-Study metric on an ambient projective space plays a central role in the construction or approximation of Kähler-Einstein metrics on algebraic varieties, and it is our hope that more general theory may shed further light on the discrete problem outlined above.

1. Hermitian preliminaries

We begin with a few remarks to fix conventions. The complex vector space

(1.1) ℂn={𝐳=(z1,…​zn)⊤:zi∈ℂ}\mathbb{C}^{n}=\{\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots z_{n})^{\top}:z_{i}\in\mathbb{C}\}

(1.2) ⟨𝐰,𝐳⟩=⟨𝐰|𝐳⟩=∑i=1nw¯i​zi\left<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}\right>=\left<\mathbf{w}|\,\mathbf{z}\right>=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\overline{w}_{i}z_{i}

which is anti-linear in the first (bra) position. Each fixed 𝐰\mathbf{w} defines a linear functional 𝐳↦⟨𝐰,𝐳⟩,\mathbf{z}\mapsto\left<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}\right>, and

(1.3) 𝐰↦⟨𝐰,∙⟩\mathbf{w}\ \mapsto\ \left<\mathbf{w},\ \hbox{\footnotesize$\bullet$}\ \right>

is an anti-linear bijective mapping h:V→V∗,h\colon V\to V^{*}, equivalently an isomorphism V≅V¯∗V\cong\overline{V}^{*} of complex vector spaces. Complex projective space is the quotient

(1.4) ℂ​ℙn−1=ℂn∖0ℂ∗,\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}=\frac{\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus 0}{\mathbb{C}^{*}},

consisting of one-dimensional subspaces of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} or rays, and is a compact topological space. For any non-zero 𝐰∈ℂn\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} the associated point in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} will be denoted by [𝐰].[\mathbf{w}]. Each such point determines a conjugate hyperplane WW defined by

(1.5) W=ℙ⁡(ker⁡h⁡(𝐰))≅ℂ​ℙn−2⊂ℂ​ℙn−1.W=\mathbb{P}(\ker h(\mathbf{w}))\cong\mathbb{CP}^{n-2}\subset\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}.

This is the geometrical content of the map h.h.

Two points [𝐰],[𝐳][\mathbf{w}],[\mathbf{z}] lie on a unique projective line 𝕃≅ℂ​ℙ1.\mathbb{L}\cong\mathbb{CP}^{1}. The associated conjugate hyperplanes W,ZW,Z intersect 𝕃\mathbb{L} in [𝐰′],[𝐳′],[\mathbf{w}^{\prime}],[\mathbf{z}^{\prime}], where

(1.6) 𝐰′=⟨𝐰,𝐳⟩​𝐰−⟨𝐰,𝐰⟩​𝐳,𝐳′=⟨𝐳,𝐳⟩​𝐰−⟨𝐳,𝐰⟩​𝐳.\mathbf{w}^{\prime}=\left<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}\right>\mathbf{w}-\left<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}\right>\mathbf{z},\hskip 23.49976pt\mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\left<\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}\right>\mathbf{w}-\left<\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}\right>\mathbf{z}.

The resulting four points, taken in the order [𝐰],[𝐳],[𝐳′],[𝐰′],[\mathbf{w}],[\mathbf{z}],[\mathbf{z}^{\prime}],[\mathbf{w}^{\prime}], have inhomogeneous coordinates

(1.7) ∞,0,−⟨𝐳,𝐳⟩/⟨𝐳,𝐰⟩,−⟨𝐰,𝐳⟩/⟨𝐰,𝐰⟩,\infty,\hskip 11.74988pt0,\hskip 11.74988pt-\big<\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}\big>/\big<\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}\big>,\hskip 11.74988pt-\left<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}\right>/\big<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}\big>,

and a real cross ratio

The Fubini-Study distance dd between the points [𝐰][\mathbf{w}] and [𝐳][\mathbf{z}] is defined by expressing the cross ratio as cos2⁡(d/2),\cos^{2}(d/2), so that

(1.9) d⁡([𝐰],[𝐳])=2​arccos⁡(|⟨𝐰,𝐳⟩|‖𝐰‖​‖𝐳‖)∈[0,π].d([\mathbf{w}],[\mathbf{z}])=2\arccos\left(\frac{|\big<\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}\big>|}{\|\mathbf{w}\|\|\mathbf{z}\|}\right)\in[0,\pi].

2. The special unitary group

The Hermitian form hh is invariant under the action of the unitary group

(2.1) U⁡(n)={X∈ℂn,n:X¯​X⊤=I}.\mathrm{U}(n)=\{X\in\mathbb{C}^{n,n}:\overline{X}\!X^{\top}=I\}.

Its centre consists of scalar multiples ei​t​Ie^{it}I that act trivially on ℂ​ℙn−1.\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}. So we consider the special unitary group

(2.2) SU⁡(n)={X∈U⁡(n):detX=1},\mathrm{SU}(n)=\{X\in\mathrm{U}(n):\det X=1\},

whose centre is ℤn=⟨e2​π​i/n​I⟩.\mathbb{Z}_{n}=\big<e^{2\pi i/n}I\big>. The next result is due to Wigner [41]; a modern treatment is given in [15].

Theorem 2.1.

The isometry group of the Fubini-Study space ℂ​ℙn−1,\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}, i.e. the group of bijections preserving the distance d,d, is generated by SU⁡(n)/ℤn\mathrm{SU}(n)/\mathbb{Z}_{n} and [𝐳]↦[𝐳¯].[\mathbf{z}]\mapsto[\overline{\mathbf{z}}].

The Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔲​(n)\mathfrak{su}(n) can (as a vector space) be defined as the tangent space TI​SU​(n)T_{I}\mathrm{SU}(n) at the identity. It consists of tangent vectors A=X˙0A=\dot{X}_{0} to curves Xt=I+t​A+O⁡(t2)X_{t}=I+tA+O(t^{2}) in U⁡(n).U(n). Thus

A matrix M∈SU⁡(n)M\in\mathrm{SU}(n) acts on 𝔰​𝔲​(n)\mathfrak{su}(n) by the adjoint representation

(2.4) A↦M​A​M−1=M​A​M⊤.A\mapsto M\!AM^{-1}=M\!AM^{\top}.

The space 𝔰​𝔲​(n)\mathfrak{su}(n) carries an invariant inner product

(2.5) ⟨A,B⟩=−tr(AB),\big<A,B\big>=-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(AB),

and SU⁡(n)\mathrm{SU}(n) itself carries a bi-invariant Riemannian invariant. We shall work with the corresponding affine space

(2.6) ℋn={A∈ℂn,n:A¯=A⊤,trA=1}\mathscr{H}_{n}=\{A\in\mathbb{C}^{n,n}:\overline{A}=A^{\top},\ \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A=1\}

(2.7) ℋn⟶≅𝔰​𝔲​(n),\mathscr{H}_{n}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cong}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ \mathfrak{su}(n),

given by A↦i⁡(A−n−1​I).A\mapsto i(A-n^{-1}I).

Example 2.2 (The Bloch sphere).

For n=2,n=2, the image of this map consists of the matrices

(2.12) (|z1|2z¯1​z2z1​z¯2|z2|2)=12​(1+ab+i​cb−i​c1−a)\left(\!\begin{array}[]{cc}|z_{1}|^{2}&\overline{z}_{1}z_{2}\\[3.0pt] z_{1}\overline{z}_{2}&|z_{2}|^{2}\end{array}\!\right)=\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{2}$}\!\left(\!\begin{array}[]{cc}1+a&b+ic\\[2.0pt] b-ic&1-a\end{array}\!\right)

But θ\theta is also the standard distance dd along the great circle on the surface of the sphere joining the endpoints of the two unit vectors.

In the example above, fix (say) the north pole p∈S2,p\in S^{2}, and consider the function κp=sin2⁡(θ/2)\kappa_{p}=\sin^{2}(\theta/2) where θ\theta is now latitude in radians. Its gradient ∇κp\nabla\kappa_{p} is tangent to the meridians joining pp to the south pole p′,p^{\prime}, whereas J⁡(∇κp)J(\nabla\kappa_{p}) is a vector field that represents rotation about p​p′.pp^{\prime}. This situation is generalized to higher dimensions as follows. The composition

(2.15) ℂ​ℙn−1⟶ℋn⟶≅𝔰​𝔲​(n),\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathscr{H}_{n}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cong}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ \mathfrak{su}(n),

For further details of various aspects of the Kählerian geometry of the space of pure quantum states, see Anandan and Aharonov [1], Ashtekar and Schilling [7], Bengtsson and Zyczkowski [8], Brody and Hughston [9], Gibbons [16], Hughston [25, 26], and Kibble [27].

3. Sets of points in projective space

We choose to begin with

Definition 3.1.

A SIC-POVM or SIC set is a collection 𝕊\mathbb{S} of n2n^{2} points [𝐳i][\mathbf{z}_{i}] in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} that are mutually equidistant, so if ‖𝐳i‖=1\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|=1 then

(3.1) |⟨𝐳i,𝐳j⟩|2=κ,i≠j,|\big<\mathbf{z}_{i},\mathbf{z}_{j}\big>|^{2}=\kappa,\hskip 23.49976pti\neq j,

for some fixed cross ratio κ∈[0,1).\kappa\in[0,1).

We can associate to [𝐳i][\mathbf{z}_{i}] the point Pi=P[𝐳i]P_{i}=P_{[\mathbf{z}_{i}]} in ℋn.\mathscr{H}_{n}. A SIC set then consists of a regular simplex embedded in

(3.2) ℋn≅𝔰​𝔲​(n)≅ℝN,N=n2−1\mathscr{H}_{n}\cong\mathfrak{su}(n)\cong\mathbb{R}^{N},\hskip 11.74988ptN=n^{2}\!-\!1

with n2n^{2} vertices {Pi}\{P_{i}\} that lie in the adjoint orbit ℂ​ℙn−1.\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}. The latter requirement is the crucial one, since a regular simplex with n2n^{2} vertices in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} is readily obtained by projecting an arbitrary orthonormal basis of ℝN+1.\mathbb{R}^{N+1}.

Do SIC sets exist?

Example 3.2.

A SIC set in ℂ​ℙ1=S2\mathbb{CP}^{1}=S^{2} is an inscribed tetrahedron in the two-sphere. Any two such tetrahedrons are congruent by SO⁡(3)=SU⁡(2)/ℤ2,\mathrm{SO}(3)=\mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}, though that does not stop us seeking the ‘neatest’ set of vertices to write down. One set is

(3.3) {[0,1],[2,1],[2,ω],[2,ω2]},\Big\{\ [0,1],\hskip 11.74988pt[\sqrt{2},1],\hskip 11.74988pt[\sqrt{2},\omega],\hskip 11.74988pt[\sqrt{2},\omega^{2}]\ \Big\},

where ω=e2​π​i/3.\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}. Another set of vertices, which is perhaps less obvious, is

(3.4) {[1,ϖ],[ϖ,1],[1,−ϖ],[ϖ,−1]},\Big\{\ [1,\varpi],\hskip 11.74988pt[\varpi,1],\hskip 11.74988pt[1,-\varpi],\hskip 11.74988pt[\varpi,-1]\ \Big\},

where ϖ=(1+i)/(1+3).\varpi=(1+i)/(1+\sqrt{3}). This second set nevertheless plays an important role, as we shall see.

If n⩾3,n\geqslant 3, any two SIC sets in ℂ​ℙn−1⊂ℝN\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} are congruent by SO⁡(N)\mathrm{SO}(N) (where N=n2−1N=n^{2}-1), but not in general by SU⁡(n).\mathrm{SU}(n).

One can present more SIC sets by generalizing the second tetrahedron (3.4). We define two cyclic groups of order n.n. Let WW be the group generated by the cyclic permutation

(3.5) [z1,z2,…,zn]↦[zn,z1,…,zn−1];[z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{n}]\mapsto[z_{n},z_{1},\ldots,z_{n-1}];

let ω=e2​π​i/n,\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}, and denote by HH the group generated by

(3.6) [z1,z2,…,zn]↦[z1,ω​z2,…,ωn−1​zn].[z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{n}]\mapsto[z_{1},\omega z_{2},\ldots,\omega^{n-1}z_{n}].

W×HW\times H acts on ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} as a subgroup of SU⁡(n)\mathrm{SU}(n) isomorphic to ℤn×ℤn.\mathbb{Z}_{n}\times\mathbb{Z}_{n}. This subgroup is sometimes called the Weyl-Heisenberg group after [40]. It can be regarded as the projectivization of an extended finite group, namely the Heisenberg group of three-by-three matrices with coefficients in the ring ℤn.\mathbb{Z}_{n}. For this reason, it is legitimate to refer to the action of W×HW\times H simply as that of the Heisenberg group. The following two results can be verified by direct calculation:

Proposition 3.3.

The orbit

(3.7) (W×H)⋅[0,1,1](W\times H)\cdot[0,1,1]

is a SIC set consisting of nine points in ℂ​ℙ2.\mathbb{CP}^{2}.

Proposition 3.4.

Let r=2r=\sqrt{2} and s=2+5.s=\sqrt{2+\sqrt{5}}. Then

(3.8) (W×H)⋅[−s−i⁡(r+s),−r+i,s+i⁡(s−r), 1+r+i](W\times H)\cdot[-s-i(r\!+\!s),\ 1\!-\!r+i,\ s+i(s\!-\!r),\ 1+r+i]

is a SIC set of sixteen points in ℂ​ℙ3.\mathbb{CP}^{3}.

An element 𝐳∈ℂn\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} such that the orbit (W×H)⋅[𝐳](W\times H)\cdot[\mathbf{z}] is a SIC set is called a fiducial vector for the action of W×H.W\times H.

In his 1999 Vienna PhD thesis [43], Zauner made a number of conjectures that extended the basic

Conjecture 3.5.

ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} possesses a SIC set for all n.n.

It is widely believed that such a set can always be realized as an orbit of W×H,W\times H, and that the number of non-congruent solutions (meaning solutions that are not related to one another by an isometry or element of SU⁡(n)\mathrm{SU}(n)) increases with n.n. There are sporadic constructions of SIC sets using different finite groups (see Remark 3.8).

Explicit algebraic solutions are known for n=2,3,4,…,15,19,24,35n=2,3,4,\ldots,15,19,24,35 and 48,48, from work of Zauner [43], Appleby [2], Renes et al. [32], Flammia [14], Grassl [18], Zhu [44], and many other authors (see [3, 11] and references cited therein). All such examples lie (up to isometry) in solvable extensions of ℚ\mathbb{Q} [4]. Extensive numerical verification has been carried out for n⩽67n\leqslant 67 (Scott and Grassl [33]).

The next result is well known, but we include it for completeness. Let {[𝐳i]}\{[\mathbf{z}_{i}]\} be a SIC set in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} and {Pi}\{P_{i}\} its image in ℋn.\mathscr{H}_{n}. Recall that tr(Pi​Pj)=κ\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(P_{i}P_{j})=\kappa if i≠j.i\neq j. Thus κ\kappa is the cross ratio or transition probability between any two points in the SIC set.

Lemma 3.6.

Any SIC set in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} satisfies κ=1/(n+1),\kappa=1/(n+1), and

(3.9) 1n​∑Pi=I.\frac{1}{n}\sum P_{i}=I.
Proof.

Define Qj=Pj−κ​I.Q_{j}=P_{j}-\kappa I. Then

(3.10) tr(Pi​Qj)={1−κi=j0i≠j\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(P_{i}Q_{j})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1-\kappa&i=j\\ 0&i\neq j\end{array}\right.

So (Pi)(P_{i}) is a basis of i​𝔲​(n)i\mathfrak{u}(n) (called a quorum) and we can set

(3.11) I=∑i=1n2ci​Pi.I=\sum_{i=1}^{n^{2}}c_{i}P_{i}.

Applying tr(Qj⋅),\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(Q_{j}\,\cdot), we get 1−κ​n=cj​(1−κ),1-\kappa n=c_{j}(1-\kappa), so all the cic_{i} are equal. To complete the proof, take the trace of (3.11). This gives

(3.12) n=n2​1−κ​n1−κ,n=n^{2}\frac{1-\kappa n}{1-\kappa},

and κ=(1−n)/(1−n2)=1/(1+n).\kappa=(1-n)/(1-n^{2})=1/(1+n). ∎

It will be convenient in our analysis of SIC sets to introduce the following.

Definition 3.7.

Two points in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} will be said to be ‘correctly separated’ if the cross ratio that they define equals 1/(n+1).1/(n+1).

Suppose that ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} admits a SIC set 𝕊.\mathbb{S}. Then, up to isometry, two points form part of a SIC set if and only if they are correctly separated. This follows from the fact that ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} is a two-point homogeneous space, meaning that there exists an isometry that maps any two points to any other two points the same distance apart [38]. The lemma above is then a key result that enables one to go some way in attempting to construct a SIC set without knowing for sure that it exists.

Remark 3.8.

Lemma 3.6 precludes the existence of four or more points of a SIC set from lying on a projective line ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} whenever n⩾3,n\geqslant 3, since their cross ratio would have to be that for n=2,n=2, namely 1/3.1/3. An application relates to the SIC set in ℂ​ℙ7\mathbb{CP}^{7} constructed by Hoggar [21]. It consists of a (ℤ2)6(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{6} orbit of 64 points that the Hopf fibration π:ℂ​ℙ7→ℍ​ℙ3\pi\colon\mathbb{CP}^{7}\to\mathbb{HP}^{3} projects down to an equal number of points in the quaternionic projective space ℍ​ℙ3.\mathbb{HP}^{3}. It would be impossible to find a SIC set in ℂ​ℙ7\mathbb{CP}^{7} with four points in each fibre of π,\pi, but we wonder whether there exists a SIC set arising from 32 points in ℍ​ℙ3\mathbb{HP}^{3} with two points in each fibre. Such questions are related to work by Armstrong et al. on twistor lifts [5].

5. Weyl-Heisenberg orbits

In this section, we show how the moment mapping (4.3) helps one to understand the action of the groups WW and HH defined in (3.5) and (3.6) with n=3.n=3. We shall see that the 𝒞\mathscr{C} plays a prominent role, and Lemma 4.2 will be the basis for the parametrization of elements of a SIC set.

Lemma 5.1.

The HH-orbit of a point [𝐳][\mathbf{z}] in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} consists of three points that are correctly separated from one another if and only if μ⁡([𝐳])∈𝒞.\mu([\mathbf{z}])\in\mathscr{C}.

Proof.

Suppose that 𝐳=𝐳(0)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}^{(0)} is a unit vector. The orbit H⋅[𝐳]H\cdot[\mathbf{z}] consists of the projective classes of the vectors

(5.1) 𝐳(0)=(z1,z2,z3),𝐳(1)=(z1,ω​z2,ω2​z3),𝐳(2)=(z1,ω2​z2,ω​z3)\mathbf{z}^{(0)}=(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}),\hskip 11.74988pt\mathbf{z}^{(1)}=(z_{1},\omega z_{2},\omega^{2}z_{3}),\hskip 11.74988pt\mathbf{z}^{(2)}=(z_{1},\omega^{2}z_{2},\omega z_{3})

generated by (3.6). We can express

(5.2) |⟨𝐳(0),𝐳(1)⟩|2=(|z1|2+ω|z2|2+ω2|z3|2)(|z1|2+ω2|z2|2+ω|z32|)|\big<\mathbf{z}^{(0)},\mathbf{z}^{(1)}\big>|^{2}=(|z_{1}|^{2}+\omega|z_{2}|^{2}+\omega^{2}|z_{3}|^{2})(|z_{1}|^{2}+\omega^{2}|z_{2}|^{2}+\omega|z_{3}^{2}|)

in the form α−β,\alpha-\beta, where

Therefore 𝐳(0)\mathbf{z}^{(0)} and 𝐳(1)\mathbf{z}^{(1)} are correctly separated if and only if α−β=1/4.\alpha-\beta=1/4. But

(5.4) α+2​β=(|z1|2+|z2|2+|z3|2)2=1,\alpha+2\beta=(|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}+|z_{3}|^{2})^{2}=1,

since 𝐳=𝐳(0)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}^{(0)} is normalized, so the condition of correct separation is α=1/2.\alpha=1/2. Since xi=|zi|2x_{i}=|z_{i}|^{2} are the Cartesian coordinates in ℝ3,\mathbb{R}^{3}, correct separation of 𝐳(0)\mathbf{z}^{(0)} and 𝐳(1)\mathbf{z}^{(1)} implies that μ⁡([𝐳])∈𝒞.\mu([\mathbf{z}])\in\mathscr{C}. This condition only depends on μ⁡([𝐳])\mu([\mathbf{z}]) since HH is a subgroup of TT and its action commutes with all the elements of T.T. Therefore if μ⁡([𝐳])∈𝒞,\mu([\mathbf{z}])\in\mathscr{C}, all three points in (5.1) will be correctly separated. ∎

Example 5.2.

Lemma 5.1 is really an assertion about the induced metric on the fibres μ−1​(p)\mu^{-1}(p) for p∈𝒞.p\in\mathscr{C}. This metric will depend crucially on the position of pp in 𝒞,\mathscr{C}, since it degenerates as pp approaches any one of the midpoints mim_{i} (over which the fibres are circles rather than 2-tori). This behaviour is illustrated in Figure 2, which provides a visualization of the fibres μ−1​(pi)\mu^{-1}(p_{i}) for i=1,2,i=1,2, where

(5.5) p1=(23,16,16),p2=(18​(3+5),14,18​(3−5)).p_{1}=\big(\hbox{\Large$\frac{2}{3}$},\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{6}$},\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{6}$}\big),\hskip 23.49976ptp_{2}=\big(\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{8}$}(3+\sqrt{5}),\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{4}$},\hbox{\Large$\frac{1}{8}$}(3-\sqrt{5})\big).

are two points of 𝒞\mathscr{C}. Note that p1p_{1} is the point diametrically opposite m1,m_{1}, whereas p2p_{2} lies between p1p_{1} and m3.m_{3}.

The coordinates used in Figure 2 are derived from the action of the maximal torus (4.1), which is represented by translation. Scalar multiplication by ω=e2​π​i/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3} on vectors in ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} generates the action of the centre ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} of SU⁡(3),\mathrm{SU}(3), so that (z1,z2,z3)(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}) and (ω​z1,ω​z2,ω​z3)(\omega z_{1},\omega z_{2},\omega z_{3}) appear as distinct points in the diagrams, although they determine the same point of ℂ​ℙ2.\mathbb{CP}^{2}. The centre is responsible for the evident three-fold symmetry, which is best represented by the hexagonal fundamental domain on the right-hand side. Comparing this with the left-hand parallogram and its translates, one sees that a 2-torus can be formed by identifying the opposite edges of a hexagon, a fact that is well known (see, for example, Thurston [37]).

Both diagrams display exactly three distinct points of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} in the closure of each coloured fundamental domain, and each of these triples of points forms an equilateral triangle. This can be seen from an inspection of the curves that are the loci of points a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 from the centre point. The latter is correctly separated from each of the other two points, and these two points are correctly separated from each other because distances are translation invariant.

We are now in a position to give a full description of those SIC sets that are orbits of the group generated by (3.5) and (3.6).

Theorem 5.3.

To summarize, any three equally-spaced points on 𝒞\mathscr{C} form the ‘base’ of a group covariant SIC set. If these are the three midpoints mim_{i} of the sides then any point in μ−1​(mi)\mu^{-1}(m_{i}) is a fiducial vector. But for a generic point p∈𝒞,p\in\mathscr{C}, the choices are restricted to nine points on the two-torus μ−1​(p).\mu^{-1}(p). As pp approaches a midpoint, these nine points become three.

Remark 5.4.

The methods of this section can be extended to the study of SIC sets in ℂ​ℙn−1\mathbb{CP}^{n-1} that arise as orbits of W×HW\times H for n>3.n>3. Using the moment mapping μ:ℂ​ℙn−1→ℝn,\mu\colon\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, one can define a subset of the simplex μ⁡(ℂ​ℙn−1)\mu(\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}) consisting of points whose inverse image contains HH-orbits of correctly-separated points. For ℂ​ℙ3\mathbb{CP}^{3} the relevant subset consists of two circular arcs inside a solid tetrahedron, but is no longer one-dimensional if n>4,n>4, as discussed by Lora Lamia [30]. For applications of the use of μ:ℂ​ℙ3→ℝ4\mu\colon\mathbb{CP}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{4} in classifying almost-Hermitian structures on manifolds of real dimension six, see Mihaylov [31].

The SIC sets in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} described above have been discussed by Renes et al. [32], Zhu [44], and various other authors. In particular, it is known that any SIC set arising from Theorem 5.3 is isometric to a midpoint solution. This can be proved by adapting the proof of Proposition 6.2 below, but we shall prove a much stronger result in this paper, namely

Theorem 5.5.

Any SIC set 𝕊\mathbb{S} in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} is congruent modulo SU⁡(3)\mathrm{SU}(3) to a midpoint solution.

In the next section, we shall work with yet another description of the isometry class of a midpoint solution, in which each circle CiC_{i} contains exactly two points of the SIC set.

Remark 6.3.

Nine points in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} are the inflection points of a non-singular cubic curve if and only if the line determined by any two of them contains a third. This being the case, there are twelve such lines altogether, on which the nine points lie by threes, with four of the twelve lines through each of the nine points, thus forming the so-called Hesse configuration {94,123}\{9_{4},12_{3}\}. For the points of 𝕊θ\mathbb{S}_{\theta} to arise in this way, and as described by Hughston [24] and Dang et al. [11], the projective line 𝕃1≅ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{L}_{1}\cong\mathbb{CP}^{1} generated [𝐳1],[𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{1}],[\mathbf{z}_{2}] must contain a third point of 𝕊θ.\mathbb{S}_{\theta}. But 𝕃1\mathbb{L}_{1} is the inverse image by μ\mu of the side of 𝒯\mathscr{T} containing m1,m_{1}, and will only contain another point if θ\theta assumes one of the values ±π/2,±π/6.\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/6. This occurs when the three red legs (the ones generated by [𝐳3][\mathbf{z}_{3}] by rotation by 2​π/32\pi/3) in Figure 3 line up with the green legs (the ones over the midpoints), and 𝕊θ\mathbb{S}_{\theta} is then itself a special midpoint solution.

Example 6.4.

The unitary transformation MM maps C3′C_{3}^{\prime} to C3.C_{3}. It permutes the elements of the SIC set (W×H)⋅[0,1,−1],(W\times H)\cdot[0,1,-1], though it fixes none of them. The matrices

(6.16) A=(010001100),B=(1000ω000ω2)A=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 1&0&0\end{array}\!\right),\hskip 11.74988ptB=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&0&0\\ 0&\omega&0\\ 0&0&\omega^{2}\end{array}\!\right)

generate WW and HH respectively, and satisfy

(6.17) M​A​M−1=ω​B,M​B​M−1=ω2​A−1​B−1.M\kern-1.0ptAM^{-1}=\omega B,\hskip 23.49976ptM\kern-1.0ptBM^{-1}=\omega^{2}A^{-1}B^{-1}.

It follows that MM is an element of the so-called Clifford group, the normalizer of W×HW\times H in U⁡(3).\mathrm{U}(3). Modulo phase, this normalizer is isomorphic to a semidirect product SL⁡(2,ℤ3)⋉(ℤ3)2\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}_{3})\ltimes(\mathbb{Z}_{3})^{2} (see Appleby [2] and Horrocks-Mumford [23]). Equation (6.17) asserts that MM induces the automorphism of W×HW\times H given by

(6.18) (0−11−1)∈SL⁡(2,ℤ3).\left(\!\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-1\\ 1&-1\end{array}\!\right)\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}_{3}).

It is conjectured that a fiducial vector can always be found in an eigenspace of some element of the Clifford group (see Zauner [43]). In the case of M,M, a computation shows that any one of its eigenvectors defines a point of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} whose orbit under W×HW\times H is a configuration of nine points arranged in nine lines. Each of the 27 pairs of points lying on one of the nine lines has a cross ratio κ=1/3,\kappa=1/3, whereas the remaining nine pairs of points have κ=0.\kappa=0. Compared to the Hesse configuration above, this means that three of the twelve triples of points are not collinear, but each of these three triples forms an orthonormal basis of ℂ3.\mathbb{C}^{3}.

Remark 6.5.

If an isometry is to fix both [𝐳1][\mathbf{z}_{1}] and [𝐳2],[\mathbf{z}_{2}], there is no ambiguity remaining in the choice of ϕ∈[−π/2,π/2)\phi\in[\!-\!\pi/2,\pi/2) in Lemma 6.1. However, we are at liberty to interchange [𝐳1][\mathbf{z}_{1}] and [𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{2}] by applying either complex conjugation or the unitary

(6.19) (100001010).\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{array}\!\right).

The former has the effect of replacing σ\sigma by −σ,-\sigma, and the latter of replacing ϕ\phi by −ϕ-\phi in (6.3). In particular, the congruence class of the unordered set 𝕊θ\mathbb{S}_{\theta} uniquely specifies |θ|.|\theta|. This fact can also be verified using a triple product that measures the signed area of the planar geodesic triangle spanned by three points. See, for example, Brody and Hughston [9] and references cited therein.

and ϕ=−ψ=±π/6,\phi=-\psi=\pm\pi/6, values that are excluded. We may therefore assume that Γ0​(Γ1+Γ2)≠0,\Gamma_{0}(\Gamma_{1}+\Gamma_{2})\neq 0, and (7.3) follows. ∎

Lemma 7.2.

If 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains the pinch point [0,1,−1][0,1,-1] as well as [0,1,−ω][0,1,-\omega] and [0,1,−ω2],[0,1,-\omega^{2}], then 𝕊\mathbb{S} is a midpoint solution.

Proof.

By hypothesis, 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains three points of the circle C1.C_{1}. If 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] is a fourth point of 𝕊,\mathbb{S}, then (7.1) is correctly separated from [0,1,−1][0,1,-1] and

(7.14) cos⁡(ϕ+23​π)−cos⁡(ϕ+43​π)=±32.\cos(\phi+\hbox{\Large$\frac{2}{3}$}\pi)-\cos(\phi+\hbox{\Large$\frac{4}{3}$}\pi)=\pm\hbox{\Large$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$}.

This implies that sinϕ=±1/2,\sin\phi=\pm 1/2, and forces 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] to lie on C2⊔C3.C_{2}\sqcup C_{3}. Therefore 𝕊\mathbb{S} lies in the disjoint union C1⊔C2⊔C3.C_{1}\sqcup C_{2}\sqcup C_{3}. ∎

One can rewrite (7.3) as

(7.15) cos⁡(σ−τ)=1−9​(1+2​cos⁡2​(ϕ−ψ))4​(4​cos2⁡ϕ​cos2⁡ψ+3​sin⁡2​ϕ​sin⁡2​ψ)=−5+4​cos⁡2​ϕ+4​cos⁡2​ψ−14​cos⁡2​ϕ​cos⁡2​ψ−6​sin⁡2​ϕ​sin⁡2​ψ4​(1+cos⁡2​ϕ+cos⁡2​ψ+cos⁡2​ϕ​cos⁡2​ψ+3​sin⁡2​ϕ​sin⁡2​ψ).\begin{array}[]{rcl}\cos(\sigma-\tau)&=&\displaystyle 1-\frac{9(1+2\cos 2(\phi-\psi))}{4(4\cos^{2}\phi\cos^{2}\psi+3\sin 2\phi\sin 2\psi)}\\[15.0pt] &=&\displaystyle\frac{-5+4\cos 2\phi+4\cos 2\psi-14\cos 2\phi\cos 2\psi-6\sin 2\phi\sin 2\psi}{4(1+\cos 2\phi+\cos 2\psi+\cos 2\phi\cos 2\psi+3\sin 2\phi\sin 2\psi)}.\end{array}

We shall convert the right-hand side into a rational function by setting

(7.16) x=tan⁡ϕ,y=tan⁡ψ.x=\tan\phi,\hskip 11.74988pty=\tan\psi.

In the light of Lemma 7.2, we assume from now on that x,yx,y are finite.

Equation (7.15) simplifies to

(7.17) cos⁡(σ−τ)=−11+9​x2+9​y2−27​x2​y2−24​x​y16​(1+3​x​y).\cos(\sigma-\tau)=\frac{-11+9x^{2}+9y^{2}-27x^{2}y^{2}-24xy}{16(1+3xy)}.

If 1+3​x​y=0,1+3xy=0, then the numerator on top of it must also vanish, so x2+y2=2/3x^{2}+y^{2}=2/3 and (x+y)2=0.(x+y)^{2}=0. Thus (as in the previous proof) x=−y=±1/3.x=-y=\pm 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}. This means that 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] lies on one of the circles C2,C3,C_{2},C_{3}, and 𝐳⁡[τ,ψ]\mathbf{z}[\tau,\psi] lies on the other, so there are no restrictions on σ\sigma and τ.\tau.

The main result of this section is the following, which establishes a criterion for the existence in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} of five points that are correctly separated from one another.

Theorem 7.3.

Suppose that 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ],𝐳⁡[τ,ψ],𝐳⁡[υ,χ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi],\mathbf{z}[\tau,\psi],\mathbf{z}[\upsilon,\chi] are three points of ℂ​ℙ2,\mathbb{CP}^{2}, a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 away from each other (and from [𝐳1],[𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{1}],[\mathbf{z}_{2}]). Set p=x+y+z,p=x+y+z, q=y​z+z​x+x​y,q=yz+zx+xy, r=x​y​z,r=xyz, where x=tan⁡ϕ,x=\tan\phi, y=tan⁡ψ,y=\tan\psi, z=tan⁡χ.z=\tan\chi. Then F⁡(p,q,r)=0F(p,q,r)=0 where

(7.18) F⁡(p,q,r)=9−22​p2+9​p4+87​q−126​p2​q+27​p4​q+298​q2−226​p2​q2+24​p4​q2+414​q3−138​p2​q3+189​q4+27​q5−3​p​r−50​p3​r−15​p5​r+88​p​q​r−48​p3​q​r+234​p​q2​r+18​p3​q2​r−144​p​q3​r+81​p​q4​r+189​r2−480​p2​r2−153​p4​r2+1398​q​r2−306​p2​q​r2+2736​q2​r2−486​p2​q2​r2+810​q3​r2+243​q4​r2−558​p​r3−486​p3​r3+2376​p​q​r3−810​p​q2​r3+567​r4−162​p2​r4+6399​q​r4+486​q2​r4+1701​p​r5+2187​r6.\begin{array}[]{c}F(p,q,r)=9-22p^{2}+9p^{4}+87q-126p^{2}q+27p^{4}q+298q^{2}-226p^{2}q^{2}\\ +24p^{4}q^{2}+414q^{3}-138p^{2}q^{3}+189q^{4}+27q^{5}-3pr-50p^{3}r-15p^{5}r\\ +88pqr-48p^{3}qr+234pq^{2}r+18p^{3}q^{2}r-144pq^{3}r+81pq^{4}r+189r^{2}\\ -480p^{2}r^{2}-153p^{4}r^{2}+1398qr^{2}-306p^{2}qr^{2}+2736q^{2}r^{2}-486p^{2}q^{2}r^{2}\\ +810q^{3}r^{2}+243q^{4}r^{2}-558pr^{3}-486p^{3}r^{3}+2376pqr^{3}-810pq^{2}r^{3}\\ +567r^{4}-162p^{2}r^{4}+6399qr^{4}+486q^{2}r^{4}+1701pr^{5}+2187r^{6}.\end{array}
Proof.

Although (7.18) is rather complicated, the existence of such an expression is a consequence of the elementary trigonometric identity

(7.19) A+B+C=0⇒cos2⁡A+cos2⁡B+cos2⁡C=1+2​cos⁡A​cos⁡B​cos⁡C,A+B+C=0\ \Rightarrow\ \cos^{2}\!A+\cos^{2}\!B+\cos^{2}\!C=1+2\cos A\cos B\cos C,

which is tailor made for (7.17). The identity itself can be proved by writing applying more standard ones to the sum A+(B+C).A+(B+C). Denote the right-hand side of (7.17) by the symmetric function c⁡(x,y).c(x,y). Then

(7.20) c​(x,y)2+c​(y,z)2+c​(z,x)2=1+2​c​(x,y)​c​(y,z)​c​(z,x).c(x,y)^{2}+c(y,z)^{2}+c(z,x)^{2}=1+2c(x,y)c(y,z)c(z,x).

This simplifes into the vanishing of the quotient

(7.21) 243​f​(x,y,z)2048​(1+3​x​y)2​(1+3​y​z)2​(1+3​z​x)2,\frac{243\,f(x,y,z)}{2048(1+3xy)^{2}(1+3yz)^{2}(1+3zx)^{2}},

in which ff is a totally symmetric polynomial. We can then use the Mathematica command 𝚂𝚢𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚝𝚛𝚒𝚌𝚁𝚎𝚍𝚞𝚌𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗\mathtt{SymmetricReduction} to express

(7.22) f⁡(x,y,z)=F⁡(p,q,r)f(x,y,z)=F(p,q,r)

as a function of the elementary symmetric polynomials, and the result follows. ∎

8. Graphical interpretation

Suppose once again that 𝕊\mathbb{S} is a SIC set in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} containing [𝐳1]=[0,1,−ω][\mathbf{z}_{1}]=[0,1,-\omega] and [𝐳2]=[0,1,−ω2],[\mathbf{z}_{2}]=[0,1,-\omega^{2}], and (in view of Lemma 7.2) not the third point [0,1,−1][0,1,-1] of C1.C_{1}. The planar parametrization (7.3) of the remaining points of 𝕊\mathbb{S} enables us to describe graphically the quest for such SIC sets. Before we do this, we prove two results that help with their classification.

Setting ϕ=−π/6\phi=-\pi/6 in (6.3) defines the circle C2,C_{2}, and ϕ=π/6\phi=\pi/6 the circle C3.C_{3}. It will be convenient to consider three more circles C−,C0,C+C_{-},C_{0},C_{+} given by σ=−2π/3\sigma=-2\pi/3, 00, 2​π/32\pi/3 respectively. Unlike C1,C2,C3,C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}, these three are not disjoint: they meet in [0,1,−1].[0,1,-1]. The circles C2,C3C_{2},C_{3} are represented by horizontal lines in ℛ,\mathscr{R}, and C−,C0,C+C_{-},C_{0},C_{+} by equally-spaced vertical lines; all five have diameter π.\pi. The lines representing C−,C0C_{-},C_{0} and C2C_{2} are visible in Figure 7.

Lemma 8.1.

If 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains a point 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] with |ϕ|=π/6|\phi|=\pi/6 then 𝕊\mathbb{S} is isometric to a midpoint solution.

Proof.

We can use the isometry (6.10) to shift all points of 𝕊\mathbb{S} by a translation parallel to the horizontal axis within our rectangle ℛ.\mathscr{R}. We may therefore assume that σ=0.\sigma=0. Suppose for definiteness that ϕ=π/6,\phi=\pi/6, so that x=1/3x=1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3} and 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]∈C3.\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi]\in C_{3}. Suppose that 𝐳⁡[τ,ψ]\mathbf{z}[\tau,\psi] is a fourth point of 𝕊,\mathbb{S}, and apply (7.17). The numerator equals

(8.1) −11+9​x2+9​y2−27​x2​y2−24​x​y=−8​(1+3​y),-11+9x^{2}+9y^{2}-27x^{2}y^{2}-24xy=-8(1+\sqrt{3}y),

and the right-hand side of (7.17) becomes −1/2-1/2 unless y=−1/3.y=-1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}. It follows that τ=±2π/3\tau=\pm 2\pi/3 or ψ=−π/6.\psi=-\pi/6. Indeed, the set of points correctly separated from [𝐳1],[\mathbf{z}_{1}], [𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{2}] and 𝐳⁡[0,π/6]\mathbf{z}[0,\pi/6] is the union C−∪C2∪C+.C_{-}\cup C_{2}\cup C_{+}. This union must now contain six points of 𝕊,\mathbb{S}, and no circle can contain more than three.

Now suppose that 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains distinct points 𝐳⁡[23​π,ψ]∈C+\mathbf{z}[\frac{2}{3}\pi,\psi]\in C_{+} and 𝐳⁡[υ,−16​π]∈C2\mathbf{z}[\upsilon,-\frac{1}{6}\pi]\in C_{2}. Then (7.17) tells us that either y=1/3y=1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3} (and so ψ=π/6\psi=\pi/6), or else

(8.2) cos⁡(23​π−υ)=−12\textstyle\cos(\frac{2}{3}\pi-\upsilon)=-\frac{1}{2}

and υ=−2π/3\upsilon=-2\pi/3 or υ=0\upsilon=0. So either the first point lies on C3C_{3}, or else the second point lies on C−⊔C0C_{-}\sqcup C_{0}. Now suppose that 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains 𝐳⁡[−23​π,ψ]∈C−\mathbf{z}[-\frac{2}{3}\pi,\psi]\in C_{-} and 𝐳⁡[23​π,χ]∈C+\mathbf{z}[\frac{2}{3}\pi,\chi]\in C_{+} This time, (7.17) yields

(8.3) (3​y2−1)​(3​z2−1)=0,(3y^{2}-1)(3z^{2}-1)=0,

and at least one of the two points is one of the last four in (6.11). We may also suppose that [0,1,−1]∉𝕊[0,1,-1]\not\in\mathbb{S} by Lemma 7.2. It then follows that 𝕊\mathbb{S} consists of [𝐳1][\mathbf{z}_{1}] and [𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{2}], the two points in C−∩(C2⊔C3),C_{-}\cap(C_{2}\sqcup C_{3}), the two points in C0∩(C2⊔C3)C_{0}\cap(C_{2}\sqcup C_{3}) and three points in C+,C_{+}, or the same thing with C−C_{-} and C+C_{+} interchanged. Applying (6.10) with x=±2π/3,x=\pm 2\pi/3, we obtain exactly the SIC set 𝕊θ\mathbb{S}_{\theta} for some θ\theta (like the one that includes the green points in Figures 6 and 7). Then the result follows from Proposition 6.2. ∎

Lemma 8.2.

Suppose that 𝕊\mathbb{S} is a SIC set that contains [𝐳1],[𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{1}],[\mathbf{z}_{2}] and 𝐳⁡[0,θ].\mathbf{z}[0,\theta]. Recall that any SIC set has this property up to isometry. If 𝕊\mathbb{S} contains distinct points 𝐳⁡[σ1,ϕ],𝐳⁡[σ2,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{1},\phi],\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{2},\phi] with σ1,σ2∈(−π,π)\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in(-\pi,\pi) then it is isometric to a midpoint solution.

Proof.

First observe that σ1+σ2=0;\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}=0; this follows by applying Lemma 7.1 in which we can set (τ,ψ)=(0,θ)(\tau,\psi)=(0,\theta) to obtain cos⁡σ1=cos⁡σ2.\cos\sigma_{1}=\cos\sigma_{2}. So take σ=σ1.\sigma=\sigma_{1}.

In view of Lemma 8.1, we may suppose that x=tan⁡ϕx=\tan\phi is different from ±1/3.\pm 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}. We can choose a sixth point 𝐳⁡[τ,ψ]\mathbf{z}[\tau,\psi] of 𝕊\mathbb{S} such that τ≠π,\tau\neq\pi, since the circle τ=π\tau=\pi can contain at most three points a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 apart. It follows from (7.17) that either 1+3​x​y=01+3xy=0 (and we can apply Lemma 8.1) or

(8.4) cos⁡(σ−τ)=cos⁡(−σ−τ).\cos(\sigma-\tau)=\cos(-\sigma-\tau).

Since σ=0\sigma=0 and σ=π\sigma=\pi do not yield distinct points, the only possibility remaining from our assumption is that τ=0.\tau=0. If t=tan⁡θt=\tan\theta and y=tan⁡ψy=\tan\psi, (7.17) implies that

(8.5) t2+y2−3​t2​y2−8​t​y−3=0.t^{2}+y^{2}-3t^{2}y^{2}-8ty-3=0.

This gives

(8.6) y=t±31∓3​t,y=\frac{t\pm\sqrt{3}}{1\mp\sqrt{3}\,t},

ψ=θ±π/3\psi=\theta\pm\pi/3 modulo π.\pi. This is the configuration of three points visible on the central vertical axis in Figure 7. All together, 𝕊\mathbb{S} now contains at most seven points including [𝐳1][\mathbf{z}_{1}] and [𝐳2],[\mathbf{z}_{2}], which is a contradiction. Using (7.17), one can in fact show that given the sixth point, either ϕ\phi or ψ\psi must equal ±π/6.\pm\pi/6. ∎

We are now in a position to illustrate the problem of finding SIC sets that contain [𝐳1][\mathbf{z}_{1}] and [𝐳2].[\mathbf{z}_{2}]. We can (and shall) assume that a third point of 𝕊\mathbb{S} is 𝐳⁡[0,θ]\mathbf{z}[0,\theta] for some fixed θ∈(−π/2,π/2).\theta\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2). This point corresponds to one on the central vertical axis of the rectangle ℛ,\mathscr{R}, and will be displayed by a black dot in the figures. We shall draw some curves to illustrate the concept of correctly separated points in ℛ,\mathscr{R}, meaning that the distance between the points they represent in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} equals 2​π/3.2\pi/3. A fourth point 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] of 𝕊\mathbb{S} will be displayed by a red dot.

In Figure 4, θ=π/16\theta=\pi/16 so that the third point 𝐳⁡[0,θ]\mathbf{z}[0,\theta] of 𝕊\mathbb{S} is close to centre of ℛ.\mathscr{R}. The black curve is the set of points 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] which are a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 from 𝐳⁡[0,θ].\mathbf{z}[0,\theta]. The remaining six points of 𝕊\mathbb{S} must therefore lie on this curve. One such example is represented by the red dot, which actually has ϕ=π/4.\phi=\pi/4. Points 𝐳⁡[τ,ψ]\mathbf{z}[\tau,\psi] a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 apart from this red point are those on the red curve (which has two components). The intersection of the black and red curves consists of points which are correctly separated from both the third and fourth points. Since there are only four of these (we require five), the value x=tan⁡ϕ=1x=\tan\phi=1 cannot in fact occur when θ=π/16.\theta=\pi/16.

The nature of the black curve is heavily dependent on the value chosen of θ\theta and t=tan⁡θ.t=\tan\theta. If 𝐳⁡[π,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\pi,\phi] is correctly separated from 𝐳⁡[0,θ]\mathbf{z}[0,\theta] and x=tan⁡ϕx=\tan\phi then

(8.7) 9​(1−3​t2)​x2+24​t​x+9​t2+5=0.9(1-3t^{2})x^{2}+24tx+9t^{2}+5=0.

Computing the roots of the discriminant as a function of t,t, (8.7) has distinct roots if and only if |t|>5/27=0.430​…|t|>\sqrt{5/27}=0.430\ldots In this case, the black curve has two connected components, and an example is visible in Figure 5 for which θ=π/7.\theta=\pi/7. This time the red point (σ,ϕ)(\sigma,\phi) is chosen (with xx approximately 4.754.75) so that there are exactly five points correctly separated from both the (black and red) third and fourth points. Subsequent analysis will show that these five points are not correctly separated from each other.

Although the fourth (red) point in Figure 4 is not admissible (nor, in fact, is that in Figure 5), Proposition 6.2 implies that there does exists a SIC set, namely 𝕊θ,\mathbb{S}_{\theta}, containing the first three points, so there must be at least six points on the black curve that are admissible. For Figures 6 and 7, we return to the value θ=π/16,\theta=\pi/16, and display these six points in green.

In Figure 6, we have chosen the fourth point 𝐳⁡[σ,ϕ]\mathbf{z}[\sigma,\phi] to be the admissible one with σ=0\sigma=0 and ϕ\phi negative. In Figure 7, we have chosen the fourth point to be one of the points of 𝕊θ\mathbb{S}_{\theta} that does not depend on θ.\theta. Recall that the top and bottom boundary of ℛ\mathscr{R} is a single point, and that the horizontal lines ϕ=±π/6\phi=\pm\pi/6 are the circles C2,C3.C_{2},C_{3}. Figure 7 illustrates the fact that any point of C2C_{2} is correctly separated from [𝐳1],[\mathbf{z}_{1}], [𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{2}] and a given point of C3,C_{3}, as we explained in the proof of Lemma 8.1.

9. Symmetrization

We suppose now that 𝕊\mathbb{S} is a SIC set containing, in addition to [𝐳1]=[0,1,−ω][\mathbf{z}_{1}]=[0,1,-\omega] and [𝐳2]=[0,1,−ω2],[\mathbf{z}_{2}]=[0,1,-\omega^{2}], four more points 𝐳⁡[σi,ϕi],\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}], i=3,4,5,6,i=3,4,5,6, with t=ϕ3,t=\phi_{3}, x=ϕ4,x=\phi_{4}, y=ϕ5,y=\phi_{5}, z=ϕ6.z=\phi_{6}.

In view of Theorem 7.3 and equation (7.21), our task is to investigate the system of polynomial equations given by

(9.1) f⁡(x,y,z)=0,f⁡(t,y,z)=0,f⁡(t,x,z)=0,f⁡(t,x,y)=0.f(x,y,z)=0,\ \ f(t,y,z)=0,\ \ f(t,x,z)=0,\ \ f(t,x,y)=0.

Since ff is itself symmetric, the whole system is invariant under the action of the group of permutations of t,x,y,z.t,x,y,z. There are refinements of Buchberger’s algorithm for dealing with symmetric ideals, but we shall adopt the technique outlined in [34]. Namely, we shall convert the system into a system four equations, each of which involves only the elementary symmetric polynomials defined by

(9.2) a=t+x+y+z,b=t​x+t​y+t​z+y​z+z​x+x​y,c=x​y​z+t​y​z+t​x​z+t​x​y,d=t​x​y​z.\begin{array}[]{l}a=t+x+y+z,\\ b=tx+ty+tz+yz+zx+xy,\\ c=xyz+tyz+txz+txy,\\ d=txyz.\end{array}

To accomplish this, first define

(9.3) F1=f⁡(x,y,z)+f⁡(t,y,z)+f⁡(t,x,z)+f⁡(t,x,y),F_{1}=f(x,y,z)+f(t,y,z)+f(t,x,z)+f(t,x,y),

and consider

(9.4) g⁡(t,x,y,z)=f⁡(t,x,y)−f⁡(t,x,z)y−z.g(t,x,y,z)=\frac{f(t,x,y)-f(t,x,z)}{y-z}.

This is a polynomial in t,x,y,z,t,x,y,z, so we can symmetrize it to get

(9.5) F2=g⁡(t,x,y,z)+g⁡(t,y,z,x)+g⁡(t,z,x,y)+g⁡(x,y,t,z)+g⁡(x,z,t,y)+g⁡(y,z,x,t).\begin{array}[]{r}F_{2}=g(t,x,y,z)+g(t,y,z,x)+g(t,z,x,y)\\ +g(x,y,t,z)+g(x,z,t,y)+g(y,z,x,t).\end{array}

Next, set

(9.6) h⁡(t,x,y,z)=g⁡(t,x,y,z)−g⁡(t,y,x,z)x−y,h(t,x,y,z)=\frac{g(t,x,y,z)-g(t,y,x,z)}{x-y},

so as to define

(9.7) F3=h⁡(t,x,y,z)+h⁡(t,y,z,x)+h⁡(t,z,x,y)+h⁡(x,y,t,z)+h⁡(x,z,t,y)+h⁡(y,x,t,z)+h⁡(z,x,y,t)+h⁡(x,y,z,t)+h⁡(y,z,x,t)+h⁡(z,y,t,x)+h⁡(y,z,t,x)+h⁡(z,x,t,y),F4=h⁡(t,x,y,z)−h⁡(x,t,y,z)t−x.\begin{array}[]{r}F_{3}=h(t,x,y,z)+h(t,y,z,x)+h(t,z,x,y)\\ +h(x,y,t,z)+h(x,z,t,y)+h(y,x,t,z)\\ +h(z,x,y,t)+h(x,y,z,t)+h(y,z,x,t)\\ +h(z,y,t,x)+h(y,z,t,x)+h(z,x,t,y),\\[10.0pt] \displaystyle F_{4}=\frac{h(t,x,y,z)-h(x,t,y,z)}{t-x}.\end{array}

Each of F1,F2,F3,F4F_{1},F_{2},F_{3},F_{4} is a symmetric polynomial in t,x,y,z,t,x,y,z, and can therefore be expressed as a polynomial in a,b,c,d.a,b,c,d. The proof of Theorem 5.5 proceeds by examination of the system

Another problem is the ambiguity of sign in the horizontal coordinate of ℛ,\mathscr{R}, and this will result in our method capturing solutions like that illustrated in Figure 8.

10. Conclusion

We shall use the theory of Gröbner bases to analyse the ideal

(10.1) I=⟨F1,F2,F3,F4⟩I=\left<F_{1},F_{2},F_{3},F_{4}\right>

of the polynomial ring ℝ⁡[a,b,c,d].\mathbb{R}[a,b,c,d]. In view of Lemma 8.1, we are not interested in solutions to (9.8) for which ±1/3\pm 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3} is a root of the polynomial

(10.2) g⁡(x)=x4−a​x3+b​x2−c​x+d.g(x)=x^{4}-ax^{3}+bx^{2}-cx+d.

Equivalently we want solutions for which

(10.3) G⁡(a,b,c,d)=81​g​(13)​g​(−13)=1−3​a2+6​b+9​b2−18​a​c−27​c2+18​d+54​b​d+81​d2\begin{array}[]{rcl}G(a,b,c,d)&=&81g(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})g(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\\[8.0pt] &=&1-3a^{2}+6b+9b^{2}-18ac-27c^{2}+18d+54bd+81d^{2}\end{array}

is non-zero. Nor are we interested in solutions of (9.8) that give rise to a repeated root of (10.2), for these can be ignored thanks to Lemma 8.2.

Using the notion of quotient ideal (see Cox et al. (10, Chap. 4, §4)) we compute the quotient I:⟨G⟩.I:\left<G\right>. This is done by finding a Gröbner basis for

(10.4) J=⟨u​F1,u​F2,u​F3,u​F4,(1−u)​G⟩J=\left<uF_{1},uF_{2},uF_{3},uF_{4},(1-u)G\right>

using a lexicographic ordering with the dummy variable uu first in the dictionary. Those basis elements that do not involve uu are necessarily divisible by GG and provide a basis for the quotient. The order of the remaining variables is also important, and we used the Mathematica command 𝚐𝚋:=𝙶𝚛𝚘𝚎𝚋𝚗𝚎𝚛𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚒𝚜⁡[𝙹,{𝚞,𝚊,𝚌,𝚋,𝚍}].\mathtt{gb:=GroebnerBasis[J,\{u,a,c,b,d\}]}. The first element 𝚐𝚋⁡[[𝟷]]/𝙶\mathtt{gb[[1]]/G} equals

(10.5) −(d−1)3​(3​d−1)3​(3+b+3​d)​(9​d−1)3​(1+3​b+9​d)3​(19+9​b+27​d),-(d-1)^{3}(3d-1)^{3}(3+b+3d)(9d-1)^{3}(1+3b+9d)^{3}(19+9b+27d),

and thus we obtain

a=±83,b=0,c=0,d=−1.a=\pm\hbox{\Large$\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}$},\ b=0,\ c=0,\ d=-1.

In the former case, ±1/3\pm 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3} is still a root of (10.2). In the latter case, the quartic has two non-real roots.

Case (iv). 19+9​b+27​d=0.19+9b+27d=0. This is in some sense the generic case. It leads to

(10.10) 16+9​a2+27​a​c−144​d=0,4194304−73728​a2−132192​a4+6561​a6−4866048​a​c−746496​a3​c+78732​a5​c−8626176​c2−699840​a2​c2+354294​a4​c2+1679616​a​c3+708588​a3​c3+1889568​c4+531441​a2​c4=0,\begin{array}[]{r}16+9a^{2}+27ac-144d=0,\\[4.0pt] 4194304-73728a^{2}-132192a^{4}+6561a^{6}-4866048ac-746496a^{3}c\\ +78732a^{5}c-8626176c^{2}-699840a^{2}c^{2}+354294a^{4}c^{2}+1679616ac^{3}\\ +708588a^{3}c^{3}+1889568c^{4}+531441a^{2}c^{4}=0,\end{array}

giving rise to a one-parameter family of solutions to (9.8). To describe this family, we fix t=tan⁡θt=\tan\theta exactly as we did in the figures of Section 9. We set

(10.11) a=t+p,b=t​p+q,c=t​q+r,d=t​ra=t+p,\ \ b=tp+q,\ \ c=tq+r,\ \ d=tr

(the notation is as in Theorem 7.3), and compute a Gröbner basis of the ideal KK generated by 19+9​b+27​d19+9b+27d and the left-hand sides of (10.10) in terms of t.t. This can be accomplished with the Mathematica command
ooo𝙶𝚛𝚘𝚎𝚋𝚗𝚎𝚛𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚒𝚜[𝙺,{𝚛,𝚚,𝚙},𝙲𝚘𝚎𝚏𝚏𝚒𝚌𝚒𝚎𝚗𝚝𝙳𝚘𝚖𝚊𝚒𝚗→𝚁𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝚊𝚕𝙵𝚞𝚗𝚌𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝚜].\mathtt{GroebnerBasis[K,\{r,q,p\},CoefficientDomain\to RationalFunctions]}.
Provided t≠0t\neq 0 and |t|≠1/3,|t|\neq 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}, the leading terms are p,q,r6.p,q,r^{6}. This means that the non-leading monomials are 1,r,r2,r3,r4,r5,1,r,r^{2},r^{3},r^{4},r^{5}, and that there exist six solutions over ℂ\mathbb{C} counting multiplicity [35].

Completion of the proof of Theorem 5.5.

Let us first summarize the argument so far. The existence of six correctly-separated points in ℂ​ℙ2,\mathbb{CP}^{2}, including the ones [𝐳1],[𝐳2][\mathbf{z}_{1}],[\mathbf{z}_{2}] we fixed from the start of Section 6 onwards, leads to a solution of the system (9.8). Lemma 8.1 allows us to dispense with cases in which one root tt of (10.2) (or, one root of x3−p​x2+q​x−r=0x^{3}-px^{2}+qx-r=0) equals ±1/3;\pm 1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}; such cases give rise to SIC sets isometric to 𝕊θ.\mathbb{S}_{\theta}.

Theorem 10.1 provides conditions for any extra solutions, and we are led to focus on Case (iv), which does supply a family of solutions to (9.8). We must show that these do not harbour an undetected SIC set. In accordance with (6.10), we can assume that a third point of 𝕊\mathbb{S} equals 𝐳⁡[0,θ]\mathbf{z}[0,\theta] and apply Lemma 8.2. The remaining six points of a SIC set would give rise to (63)=20\binom{6}{3}=20 solutions for each fixed x.x. But Case (iv) provides at most six sets of roots. ∎

We can now be certain that the solutions in Case (iv) are not SIC sets. For any given rational value of t,t, the solutions are roots of polynomials whose coefficients are known exactly. Experimentally, the number of real solutions varies from two to five according to the following table:

real solutionsrange2|t|<0.189830.1899<|t|<0.438650.4387<|t|<1/341/3<|t|<1.154631.1547<|t|\begin{array}[]{|c|c|}\hline\cr\hbox{real solutions}&\hbox{range}\\ \hline\cr\hline\cr 2&\hphantom{0.11<}|t|<0.1898\\ \hline\cr 3&\hskip 11.74988pt0.1899<|t|<0.4386\\ \hline\cr 5&0.4387<|t|<1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}\\ \hline\cr 4&1/\kern-2.0pt\sqrt{3}<|t|<1.1546\\ \hline\cr 3&1.1547<|t|\\ \hline\cr\end{array}

Although not SIC sets, these solutions validate (9.8) by virtue of ‘cross-field passes’ of the type described below. Their changing number as |t||t| increases reflects the transitional nature of the curves displayed in Figures 4 to 7.

Example 10.2.

Take (a,b,c,d)=(0,−22/9,c,1/9)(a,b,c,d)=(0,-22/9,c,1/9) where cc is given by (10.9) with both minus signs. Then (10.2) becomes

(10.12) 27​x4−66​x2+8​26−2​97​x+3=0,27x^{4}-66x^{2}+8\sqrt{\smash{26-2\sqrt{97}}\vphantom{I^{I}}}x+3=0,

and has four real roots, namely x3=t=−1.687​…x_{3}=t=-1.687\ldots and

(10.13) x=x4=−0.109​…y=x5=0.442​…z=x6=1.354​…x=x_{4}=-0.109\ldots\hskip 11.74988pty=x_{5}=0.442\ldots\hskip 11.74988ptz=x_{6}=1.354\ldots

Let ϕi=arctan⁡xi.\phi_{i}=\arctan x_{i}. Set σ3=0,\sigma_{3}=0, but for i=4,5,6i=4,5,6 choose σi>0\sigma_{i}>0 such that 𝐳⁡[σi,ϕi]\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}] is correctly separated from 𝐳⁡[0,ϕ3].\mathbf{z}[0,\phi_{3}]. Then [𝐳1],[𝐳2],𝐳⁡[0,ϕ3][\mathbf{z}_{1}],[\mathbf{z}_{2}],\mathbf{z}[0,\phi_{3}] are all a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 from each of the six points 𝐳⁡[±σi,ϕi]\mathbf{z}[\pm\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}] for i=4,5,6.i=4,5,6. Moreover, the pairs

(10.14) 𝐳⁡[σ4,ϕ4],𝐳⁡[σ5,ϕ5];𝐳⁡[σ4,ϕ4],𝐳⁡[σ6,ϕ6];𝐳⁡[σ5,ϕ5],𝐳⁡[−σ6,ϕ6];𝐳⁡[−σ4,ϕ4],𝐳⁡[−σ5,ϕ5];𝐳⁡[−σ4,ϕ4],𝐳⁡[−σ6,ϕ6];𝐳⁡[−σ5,ϕ5],𝐳⁡[σ6,ϕ6]\begin{array}[]{lll}\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{4},\phi_{4}],\ \mathbf{z}[\sigma_{5},\phi_{5}];&\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{4},\phi_{4}],\ \mathbf{z}[\sigma_{6},\phi_{6}];&\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{5},\phi_{5}],\ \mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{6},\phi_{6}];\\[3.0pt] \mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{4},\phi_{4}],\mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{5},\phi_{5}];&\mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{4},\phi_{4}],\mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{6},\phi_{6}];&\mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{5},\phi_{5}],\ \mathbf{z}[\sigma_{6},\phi_{6}]\end{array}

are a distance 2​π/32\pi/3 apart. This does not contradict Lemma 8.2 because 𝐳⁡[−σi,ϕi]\mathbf{z}[-\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}] and 𝐳⁡[σi,ϕi]\mathbf{z}[\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}] are not correctly separated. All together, we have constructed nine points in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} for which 27 of the (92)\binom{9}{2} pairs are correctly separated, though the resulting configuration is less symmetrical than that of Example 6.4. The seven points 𝐳⁡[±σi,ϕi]\mathbf{z}[\pm\sigma_{i},\phi_{i}] are shown in Figure 8; distinguishing a different root x3x_{3} from the list (10.13) would give a different picture of the same phenomenon.
